subject: physics

items.q: A cell has an emf of 1.5 V. What does this mean?
items.correct: For each coulomb passing through the cell, 1.5 J is transferred to electrical energy.
items.misconception: The cell holds a store of 1.5 C of charge, which it releases into the circuit.
items.why:
Everyday language speaks of 'charging' a battery and a battery 'running out', and the fuel-tank picture of a battery is taught informally from an early age. Charge is conserved and is not stored up in a cell: as much charge enters one terminal each second as leaves the other. The cell transfers chemical energy to the charge carriers that are already in the circuit. A 'flat' cell has used up its chemical reactants, not its charge.

Working: ε = W/q, so the energy transferred per coulomb is W = εq = 1.5 V × 1 C = 1.5 J (1 V = 1 J C⁻¹).
items.specStatementText: that cells provide a source of emf
items.random_wrong: The cell pushes each coulomb of charge around the circuit with a force of 1.5 N.
items.working: ε = W/q, so the energy transferred per coulomb is W = εq = 1.5 V × 1 C = 1.5 J (1 V = 1 J C⁻¹).

items.q: A chemical cell and a solar cell are each used as the energy source in a circuit. Which describes the main energy transfer in each?
items.correct: Chemical cell: chemical energy to electrical. Solar cell: energy of light to electrical.
items.misconception: Chemical cell: stored electrical energy is let out. Solar cell: light to electrical.
items.why: Batteries are sold and discussed as stores of 'electricity' or 'power', and the idea of storing electrical energy directly seems simpler than chemical reactions. The energy in a chemical cell is chemical energy of its reactants. When the circuit is complete, reactions at the electrodes transfer this chemical energy into electrical energy, doing work on the charge carriers.
items.specStatementText: chemical cells and solar cells as the energy source in circuits
items.random_wrong: Chemical cell: chemical energy to electrical. Solar cell: the Sun's heat to electrical.

items.q: A student writes: 'For a garden lamp that must shine all night, a solar cell is a better energy source than a chemical cell in every way.' Which evaluation of this claim is correct?
items.correct: Wrong: sunlight is renewable, but a solar cell gives no output at night, so a storage cell is needed.
items.misconception: Right: the solar cell stores the energy of the light it absorbs by day and releases it to the lamp at night.
items.why: Solar garden lights and calculators work after dark because they contain a rechargeable cell, which is hidden; students attribute the storage to the visible solar cell. The shared word 'cell' reinforces the idea that a solar cell is a kind of battery. A solar cell is an energy transducer, not a store. Its output is proportional to the light intensity at that moment and is zero in darkness. Any device that works at night on solar energy has a separate storage device charged during the day.
items.specStatementText: chemical cells and solar cells as the energy source in circuits
items.random_wrong: Right: the Sun is a renewable source, so a solar cell gives a steady output at all times, by day or night.

items.q: A student wants to measure the current in a lamp and the pd across it, but connects the meters the wrong way round. The circuit is: a cell, a voltmeter and the lamp connected in series in a single loop, with an ammeter connected in parallel with the lamp. Both meters are ideal. What does the student observe?
items.correct: The lamp is off, the ammeter reads zero and the voltmeter reads the emf of the cell.
items.misconception: The lamp is off and both meters read zero, as there is no current in the circuit.
items.why: Students first meet pd as 'the voltage across a component that has a current in it', and V = IR seems to say that I = 0 means V = 0 everywhere. V = IR gives zero pd only across a component with finite resistance and no current. Across a gap (infinite resistance) the pd can be large with zero current. Apply the loop rule: the pds around a loop must add up to the emf.
items.specStatementText: that circuit diagrams represent the arrangement of components in a circuit
items.random_wrong: The ammeter short-circuits the lamp, so a very large current flows through the ammeter.

items.q: A steady current of 0.40 A flows in a copper wire for 3.0 minutes. The magnitude of the charge on an electron is e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. How many electrons pass a point in the wire in this time?
items.why:
Stems often give times in minutes or hours for realism, and students copy the number without checking its unit. Convert every quantity to SI units before substituting: 1 minute = 60 s. The ampere is a coulomb per second, not per minute.

Working: Δt = 3.0 min = 180 s. Δq = IΔt = (0.40 A)(180 s) = 72 C. N = Δq/e = 72 C / (1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C) = 4.5 × 10²⁰ electrons.
items.specStatementText: direct current (dc) I as a flow of charge carriers as given by I = Δq/Δt

items.q: A copper wire forms part of a circuit carrying a steady direct current. Which statement about the charge carriers in the wire is correct?
items.correct: Free electrons drift slowly, in the opposite direction to the conventional current.
items.misconception: Electrons travel at close to the speed of light, so a lamp lights at the instant the switch closes.
items.why: The instant response of a lamp suggests that something travels from the cell to the lamp very fast, and the speed of the signal is confused with the speed of the carriers. The carriers are already in the wire, all round the circuit. When the circuit is closed they all begin to drift at once, slowly. It is the field (the signal), not each electron, that travels at a large fraction of the speed of light.
items.specStatementText: direct current (dc) I as a flow of charge carriers as given by I = Δq/Δt
items.random_wrong: Protons move along the wire, in the same direction as the conventional current.

items.q: A steady current of 0.50 A flows through a small electric motor for 2.0 minutes. In this time, 360 J of energy is transferred from electrical energy to other forms in the motor. What is the potential difference across the motor?
items.why:
In everyday speech 'electricity', 'current', 'charge' and 'power' are used interchangeably, and students form one undifferentiated idea of 'electricity'. Charge (C) is an amount; current (A = C s⁻¹) is a rate. The charge that passes in a time Δt is Δq = IΔt, so the time must always be used.

Working: q = IΔt = (0.50 A)(2.0 × 60 s) = 60 C. V = W/q = 360 J / 60 C = 6.0 V.
items.specStatementText: that the electric potential difference V is the work done per unit charge on moving a positive charge between two points along the path of the current as given by V = W/q

items.q: A battery of emf 9.0 V, a switch and a lamp are connected in series. The switch is open. An ideal voltmeter is connected first across the switch and then across the lamp. What are the two readings?
items.correct: Across the switch 9.0 V; across the lamp 0 V
items.misconception: Across the switch 4.5 V; across the lamp 4.5 V
items.why:
Early examples use identical lamps in series, where the pd does divide equally, and the special case becomes a rule. The current is the same in series components, so V = IR is largest where R is largest. Use V₁ = V × R₁/(R₁ + R₂).

Working: No current flows, so V_lamp = IR = 0 and the pd across any internal resistance is 0. Loop rule: ε = V_switch + V_lamp, so V_switch = 9.0 V − 0 = 9.0 V.
items.specStatementText: that the electric potential difference V is the work done per unit charge on moving a positive charge between two points along the path of the current as given by V = W/q
items.random_wrong: Across both the switch and the lamp 0 V
items.working: No current flows, so V_lamp = IR = 0 and the pd across any internal resistance is 0. Loop rule: ε = V_switch + V_lamp, so V_switch = 9.0 V − 0 = 9.0 V.

items.q: Copper is a good electrical conductor and polythene is an insulator. Which statement explains the difference?
items.correct: Copper has electrons free to move through it; polythene's electrons are bound to its molecules.
items.misconception: Copper contains charged particles, but polythene contains no charged particles at all.
items.why: Students are told that metals conduct 'because they have electrons', and infer that materials that do not conduct have none. All matter contains electrons. Conduction needs charge carriers that are free to move through the material. In a metal some electrons are delocalized; in an insulator such as polythene, every electron is bound in a covalent bond or an atom.
items.specStatementText: the properties of electrical conductors and insulators in terms of mobility of charge carriers
items.random_wrong: Copper has protons that are free to move; polythene's protons are all held in place.

items.q: What is the origin of the electrical resistance of a metal wire?
items.correct: Free electrons collide with the vibrating lattice ions, transferring energy to them.
items.misconception: Some of the free electrons are absorbed by the metal atoms, so fewer leave than enter.
items.why: Everyday talk of 'using electricity' merges current and energy; the lamp 'uses' something, and current is the quantity students can name. Charge is conserved, so in a series loop the current is the same everywhere. What the lamp takes is energy from the charge carriers: the pd across it measures the energy transferred per unit charge.
items.specStatementText: electric resistance and its origin
items.random_wrong: The electrons rub against the surface of the wire, like water flowing along a pipe.

items.q: The I–V characteristic of a filament lamp is plotted with current I on the vertical axis and pd V on the horizontal axis. Up to 0.10 V the graph is a straight line through the origin, and at 0.10 V the current is 0.050 A. At 6.0 V the current is 0.50 A, and the tangent to the curve at this point has a gradient of 0.040 A V⁻¹. What is the resistance of the lamp at 6.0 V, and how is it found?
items.correct: 12 Ω, from V/I using the pd and current at 6.0 V
items.misconception: 25 Ω, from the reciprocal of the tangent's gradient
items.why:
For an ohmic conductor the inverse gradient and V/I are equal, so the gradient method is learned on straight lines through the origin and then applied to curves. Always use R = V/I with the pd and current at the point. For a filament lamp the tangent at a point is steeper in V/I terms than the chord from the origin, so the gradient method gives the wrong value.

Working: R = V/I at the point = 6.0 V / 0.50 A = 12 Ω.
items.specStatementText: electrical resistance R as given by R = V/I
items.random_wrong: 2.0 Ω, from V/I on the straight part near the origin
items.working: R = V/I at the point = 6.0 V / 0.50 A = 12 Ω.

items.q: A copper cable has length 5.0 m and diameter 1.0 mm. The resistivity of copper is 1.7 × 10⁻⁸ Ω m. What is the resistance of the cable?
items.why:
Wire sizes are quoted as diameters (measured with a micrometer screw gauge), while the area formula uses the radius. Write r = d/2 before calculating the area, or use A = πd²/4.

Working: r = d/2 = 0.50 mm = 5.0 × 10⁻⁴ m. A = πr² = π(5.0 × 10⁻⁴ m)² = 7.85 × 10⁻⁷ m². R = ρL/A = (1.7 × 10⁻⁸ Ω m)(5.0 m)/(7.85 × 10⁻⁷ m²) = 0.108 Ω ≈ 1.1 × 10⁻¹ Ω.
items.specStatementText: resistivity as given by ρ = RA/L

items.q: Wire X has resistance R and is made of a material of resistivity ρ. Wire Y is made of the same material at the same temperature, but it is twice as long as X and has twice the diameter of X. What are the resistance and the resistivity of wire Y?
items.correct: resistance R/2, resistivity ρ
items.misconception: resistance R, resistivity ρ
items.why:
Students remember that area 'depends on the radius' and multiply by it once, or treat doubling the diameter as doubling the area. Always square the radius: A = πr². Doubling the diameter quadruples the area and so quarters the resistance of a wire of given length.

Working: R = ρL/A with A = πd²/4. For Y: L_Y = 2L and A_Y = 4A, so R_Y = ρ(2L)/(4A) = ½ ρL/A = R/2. ρ is a property of the material, so ρ_Y = ρ.
items.specStatementText: resistivity as given by ρ = RA/L
items.random_wrong: resistance R/2, resistivity ρ/2
items.working: R = ρL/A with A = πd²/4. For Y: L_Y = 2L and A_Y = 4A, so R_Y = ρ(2L)/(4A) = ½ ρL/A = R/2. ρ is a property of the material, so ρ_Y = ρ.

items.q: Which is a statement of Ohm's law?
items.correct: The current in a conductor is proportional to the pd across it, provided its temperature is constant.
items.misconception: Every conductor obeys V = IR, so the current in any conductor is proportional to the pd.
items.why: The equation V = IR is widely labelled 'Ohm's law' in textbooks and on websites, so the definition of resistance and the law are merged. Keep the two ideas separate. For any component, R = V/I at each point. Ohm's law holds only if that ratio stays constant as V changes (a metal at constant temperature). A filament lamp has a resistance at every pd but does not obey Ohm's law.
items.specStatementText: Ohm’s law
items.random_wrong: The resistance of a conductor is proportional to the pd across it, at constant temperature.

items.q: Three components X, Y and Z are tested. The currents at pds of 1.0 V, 2.0 V and 4.0 V are: X — 0.10 A, 0.20 A, 0.40 A; Y — 0.05 A, 0.15 A, 0.35 A; Z — 0.20 A, 0.30 A, 0.40 A. Which of the components are ohmic, and why?
items.correct: X only: V/I has the same value at every reading.
items.misconception: X and Y: each gives a straight-line graph of I against V.
items.why: 'Ohmic means a straight-line graph' is the short version students memorize; the condition 'through the origin' is dropped. Ohm's law is a proportionality: I ∝ V. Test it by checking that V/I is the same at every data point, or that the straight line passes through the origin.
items.specStatementText: the ohmic and non-ohmic behaviour of electrical conductors, including the heating effect of resistors
items.random_wrong: None of them: V/I should double as V doubles, and does not.

items.q: As the pd across a filament lamp is increased, the ratio V/I for the lamp increases. Which explanation is correct?
items.correct: The filament heats up; its ions vibrate more, so electrons collide with them more often.
items.misconception: The filament expands as it heats up, and its extra length increases its resistance.
items.why: R = ρL/A is the first formula students reach for, and expansion is a familiar effect of heating, so 'longer means more resistance' seems a natural explanation. Expansion changes L and A together: L increases by a fraction x and A by about 2x, so L/A falls slightly. The resistance of a filament rises several-fold because the lattice ions vibrate more, making electron–ion collisions more frequent.
items.specStatementText: the ohmic and non-ohmic behaviour of electrical conductors, including the heating effect of resistors
items.random_wrong: More of the current is used up in the filament at higher pd, so less passes through it.

items.q: A steady current of 0.25 A flows in a 24 Ω resistor for 2.0 minutes. How much energy is dissipated in the resistor?
items.why:
P = IV is remembered correctly, and students then substitute V = IR or I = V/R incompletely, dropping one factor. Derive the forms each time: P = IV with V = IR gives P = I × IR = I²R. Check the units: I × R gives volts, not watts.

Working: P = I²R = (0.25 A)²(24 Ω) = 1.5 W. t = 2.0 min = 120 s. E = Pt = (1.5 W)(120 s) = 180 J.
items.specStatementText: electrical power P dissipated by a resistor as given by P = IV = I²R = V²/R

items.q: A 4.0 Ω resistor and an 8.0 Ω resistor are connected in parallel across a dc supply. Which resistor dissipates more power, and why?
items.correct: The 4.0 Ω resistor dissipates twice as much, since both have the same pd and P = V²/R.
items.misconception: The 8.0 Ω resistor dissipates twice as much, since P = I²R and its resistance is larger.
items.why:
P = I²R is the most-used form, and students apply it without checking whether the current is the same in both components. Choose the form of the power equation in which the other quantity is common to both components: I²R for series, V²/R for parallel.

Working: V is the same for both. P = V²/R, so P₄/P₈ = (V²/4.0)/(V²/8.0) = 2.
items.specStatementText: electrical power P dissipated by a resistor as given by P = IV = I²R = V²/R
items.random_wrong: Both dissipate the same power, since each has the same pd and the current splits equally.
items.working: V is the same for both. P = V²/R, so P₄/P₈ = (V²/4.0)/(V²/8.0) = 2.

items.q: A 12 V dc supply of negligible internal resistance is connected to a 4.0 Ω resistor in series with a parallel combination of a 6.0 Ω resistor and a 12 Ω resistor. What is the current in the 12 Ω resistor?
items.why:
Symmetrical examples with identical parallel lamps are used first, and the equal split is generalized. Each branch has the same pd, so I = V/R in each branch: halving the resistance doubles the branch current. Only identical branches share equally.

Working: R_p = (1/6.0 + 1/12)⁻¹ = 4.0 Ω. R_total = 4.0 + 4.0 = 8.0 Ω. I = 12 V / 8.0 Ω = 1.5 A. V_p = IR_p = 1.5 × 4.0 = 6.0 V. I₁₂ = 6.0 V / 12 Ω = 0.50 A.
items.specStatementText: the combinations of resistors in series and parallel circuits [table] Series circuits: I = I₁ = I₂ = …; V = V₁ + V₂ + …; R_s = R₁ + R₂ + … Parallel circuits: I = I₁ + I₂ + …; V = V₁ = V₂ = …; 1/R_p = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂ + …

items.q: Two identical filament lamps P and Q are connected in series with a cell of negligible internal resistance, in the order: positive terminal, lamp P, lamp Q, negative terminal. How do the brightnesses of the lamps compare?
items.correct: They are equally bright, and each is dimmer than a single lamp on the cell.
items.misconception: They are equally bright, and each is as bright as a single lamp on the cell.
items.why: Students picture the cell as a pump that delivers a fixed amount of 'electricity' per second, and the constant-current model feels natural when only one circuit is ever used with a given battery. What a cell provides (approximately) is a fixed emf. The current depends on the circuit: adding a lamp in series decreases the current; adding one in parallel increases the current from the cell. Always work out the current from the emf and the total resistance.
items.specStatementText: the combinations of resistors in series and parallel circuits [table] Series circuits: I = I₁ = I₂ = …; V = V₁ + V₂ + …; R_s = R₁ + R₂ + … Parallel circuits: I = I₁ + I₂ + …; V = V₁ = V₂ = …; 1/R_p = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂ + …
items.random_wrong: P is brighter, since some of the current is used up in P before it reaches Q.

items.q: A filament lamp A is connected across a cell of negligible internal resistance. An identical lamp B is then connected in parallel with A. What happens to the brightness of A and to the current from the cell?
items.correct: A is unchanged in brightness, and the current from the cell doubles.
items.misconception: A becomes dimmer, since the pd across A is now shared with lamp B.
items.why: Students learn 'the pd is shared' in series circuits and do not distinguish series from parallel connections when applying it. For parallel branches V = V₁ = V₂ = …. With a supply of negligible internal resistance, adding a branch leaves the pd across the others unchanged; it is the total current that changes.
items.specStatementText: the combinations of resistors in series and parallel circuits [table] Series circuits: I = I₁ = I₂ = …; V = V₁ + V₂ + …; R_s = R₁ + R₂ + … Parallel circuits: I = I₁ + I₂ + …; V = V₁ = V₂ = …; 1/R_p = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂ + …
items.random_wrong: A becomes dimmer, since the cell's current is now shared between two lamps.

items.q: A battery of emf 9.0 V and internal resistance 0.50 Ω is connected to a 4.0 Ω resistor. What is the terminal potential difference of the battery?
items.why:
Most circuit problems before internal resistance is taught assume an ideal cell, and cells are labelled with their emf ('1.5 V') as if that were the pd they always give. Model a real cell as an emf ε in series with a resistance r. The current passes through r, so there is a pd Ir inside the cell, and the terminal pd is ε − Ir.

Working: I = ε/(R + r) = 9.0 V / (4.0 Ω + 0.50 Ω) = 2.0 A. V = IR = (2.0 A)(4.0 Ω) = 8.0 V; check: ε − Ir = 9.0 − (2.0)(0.50) = 8.0 V.
items.specStatementText: that electric cells are characterized by their emf ε and internal resistance r as given by ε = I(R + r)

items.q: An ideal voltmeter is connected across the terminals of a battery. With nothing else connected it reads 6.0 V. Identical 10 Ω resistors are then connected across the terminals one at a time, each in parallel with those already there. With one, two and three resistors connected, the voltmeter reads 5.7 V, 5.5 V and 5.2 V. When the resistors are removed, the reading returns at once to 6.0 V. Which explanation of the falling readings is correct?
items.correct: The battery supplies more current, so the pd across its internal resistance increases.
items.misconception: The battery's emf falls, since each extra resistor draws on more of its emf.
items.why: Students treat emf and terminal pd as the same quantity, and the idea that 'more load uses up more of the battery' seems natural. When the load is removed, the terminal pd returns at once to its no-load value, which shows that the emf has not changed. The fall under load is the pd Ir across the internal resistance.
items.specStatementText: that electric cells are characterized by their emf ε and internal resistance r as given by ε = I(R + r)
items.random_wrong: The 6.0 V is shared among more resistors, so the voltmeter gets a smaller share.

items.q: An NTC thermistor is warmed, and separately a light-dependent resistor (LDR) is moved into brighter light. How does the resistance of each change?
items.correct: Both fall, since more charge carriers are released in each device.
items.misconception: The thermistor's rises, as in a hot metal wire; the LDR's falls.
items.why: Students learn that metals' resistance increases with temperature (the filament lamp) and generalize it to all components. A thermistor is a semiconductor, not a metal. Heating increases the number of mobile charge carriers far more than it increases collisions, so its resistance falls.
items.specStatementText: that resistors can have variable resistance.
items.random_wrong: The thermistor's falls; the LDR's rises, as it resists brighter light.

items.q: A potentiometer has a uniform resistance track connected across a 9.0 V dc supply of negligible internal resistance. An ideal voltmeter is connected between one end of the track and the sliding contact, which is one third of the way along the track from that end. What does the voltmeter read?
items.why:
Students first meet pd with one component across one cell, where the component's pd does equal the supply's, and carry this over to every circuit. Use the loop rule: around any loop, the sum of the pds equals the emf. For series components the pd divides in proportion to resistance; only parallel branches directly across the supply share its whole pd.

Working: The section of track between the end and the slider has 1/3 of the total resistance. Series parts share the pd in proportion to resistance: V = 9.0 V × 1/3 = 3.0 V.
items.specStatementText: that resistors can have variable resistance.
items.working: The section of track between the end and the slider has 1/3 of the total resistance. Series parts share the pd in proportion to resistance: V = 9.0 V × 1/3 = 3.0 V.

items.q: A cell of emf 6.0 V drives a steady current of 0.25 A through a lamp for 2.0 minutes. How much energy does the cell transfer from its chemical store to the charge that passes through it in this time?
items.why:
Volts, watts and joules all describe 'how much electricity' in everyday use, and appliances are labelled with both volts and watts. Distinguish the three: V = W/q (per coulomb), P = W/t (per second), and W itself (joules). They are linked by P = IV.

Working: Charge passing: q = IΔt = 0.25 A × (2.0 × 60 s) = 30 C. Emf is the energy transferred per unit charge, ε = W/q, so W = εq = 6.0 V × 30 C = 180 J.
items.specStatementText: that cells provide a source of emf
items.working: Charge passing: q = IΔt = 0.25 A × (2.0 × 60 s) = 30 C. Emf is the energy transferred per unit charge, ε = W/q, so W = εq = 6.0 V × 30 C = 180 J.

items.q: Two resistors, each of resistance 100 kΩ, are connected in series across a 6.0 V supply of negligible internal resistance. A voltmeter that is not ideal, with a constant resistance of 100 kΩ, is connected across one of the resistors. What does the voltmeter read?
items.why:
Meters are introduced as measuring instruments rather than as circuit components with their own resistance, and the circuit diagram conventions for placing them are learned as rules without reasons. Treat every meter as a component: an ideal ammeter is a zero-resistance wire and an ideal voltmeter is a break in the circuit (infinite resistance). Redraw the circuit with those replacements to see what it actually does.

Working: The voltmeter in parallel with one 100 kΩ resistor gives 1/R_p = 1/100 + 1/100, R_p = 50 kΩ. This is in series with the other 100 kΩ, total 150 kΩ. The pd divides in proportion to resistance: V = 6.0 V × 50/150 = 2.0 V.
items.specStatementText: that circuit diagrams represent the arrangement of components in a circuit
items.working: The voltmeter in parallel with one 100 kΩ resistor gives 1/R_p = 1/100 + 1/100, R_p = 50 kΩ. This is in series with the other 100 kΩ, total 150 kΩ. The pd divides in proportion to resistance: V = 6.0 V × 50/150 = 2.0 V.

items.q: A copper wire and a solution of sodium chloride form part of the same series circuit, and a steady current flows in both. What are the charge carriers in the wire and in the solution?
items.correct: Free electrons in the wire; in the solution, positive ions and negative ions that move through it in opposite directions.
items.misconception: Free electrons in the wire and also in the solution, because a current is a flow of electrons in any conductor.
items.why: Almost every introductory example is a metal wire, so 'current' and 'flow of electrons' become synonyms; students have rarely met a conductor whose carriers are ions. Define current as the rate of flow of charge, I = Δq/Δt, and ask what is free to move in each material: delocalized electrons in a metal, ions in a molten salt or a solution, both contributing to the same current.
items.specStatementText: the properties of electrical conductors and insulators in terms of mobility of charge carriers
items.random_wrong: Protons in the wire, moving from the positive terminal to the negative; positive and negative ions in the solution.

items.q: A constant pd is applied across a metal wire, so an electric field acts on the free electrons. Why do the electrons drift along the wire at a constant average velocity rather than accelerating continuously?
items.correct: They gain speed between collisions with the lattice ions but lose it again at each collision.
items.misconception: Friction between the electrons and the inner surface of the wire balances the force from the field.
items.why: The water-in-pipes analogy used to introduce current is extended too far, and 'friction' is the everyday word for anything that opposes motion. The current flows through the whole cross-section of the metal, not along its surface. Resistance comes from electron–lattice-ion collisions throughout the volume, which is why R is proportional to L/A.
items.specStatementText: electric resistance and its origin
items.random_wrong: Collisions with the other electrons crowding through the wire keep them all moving at one speed.

items.q: The pd across and the current in four components are measured. W: 9.0 V and 3.0 A. X: 2.0 V and 4.0 A. Y: 3.0 V and 0.60 A. Z: 0.80 V and 0.20 A. Which component has the greatest resistance?
items.correct: Y
items.misconception: W
items.why:
Students read a defining equation as a causal rule, holding I fixed in their minds while V changes. In R = V/I, V and I are not independent: for an ohmic conductor at constant temperature, doubling V doubles I, so V/I is unchanged. That constancy is exactly what Ohm's law states.

Working: R = V/I for each: W: 9.0/3.0 = 3.0 Ω; X: 2.0/4.0 = 0.50 Ω; Y: 3.0/0.60 = 5.0 Ω; Z: 0.80/0.20 = 4.0 Ω. The greatest is component Y, 5.0 Ω.
items.specStatementText: electrical resistance R as given by R = V/I
items.random_wrong: X

items.q: A student measures the resistance of a length of metal wire as 5.0 Ω, using a pd of 1.0 V. The student claims that, by Ohm's law, the current in the wire will be 2.4 A when the pd is increased to 12 V. Which statement about this claim is correct?
items.correct: It holds only if the wire is at the same temperature at 12 V as it was at 1.0 V.
items.misconception: It holds, because 5.0 Ω is a fixed property of this wire whatever pd is applied to it.
items.why:
Fixed resistors, whose resistance is printed on them, are the first components students meet, and many problems treat R as a given constant. Resistance is defined at each operating point by R = V/I. It is constant only for an ohmic conductor at constant temperature. For other components, find R from the pd and current under the conditions in question.

Working: If R stays 5.0 Ω, I = V/R = 12 V / 5.0 Ω = 2.4 A. Ohm's law (I ∝ V) holds for a metal only at constant temperature. At 12 V the wire would dissipate P = V²/R = 144/5.0 = 29 W, far more than the 0.20 W at 1.0 V, so it will heat up and its resistance rise unless it is kept at the same temperature.
items.specStatementText: Ohm’s law
items.random_wrong: It holds only if the wire is a metal, because every metal conductor obeys Ohm's law.

items.q: The circuit diagram shows two lamps, L₁ and L₂, of different resistances connected in parallel to a cell, together with ammeters A₁ and A₂. Which statement about the ammeter readings is correct?
items.correct: A₁ reads more than A₂, because A₁ measures the total current and A₂ measures only the current in L₂.
items.misconception: A₁ and A₂ give the same reading, because the current is the same at every point in the circuit.
items.why: 'Current is the same everywhere' is taught as the correction to the current-used-up idea, and students then apply it to parallel circuits as well. Charge is conserved at a junction: the current in equals the sum of the currents out (I = I₁ + I₂ + …). So each branch carries only part of the total current.
items.specStatementText: that circuit diagrams represent the arrangement of components in a circuit
items.random_wrong: A₂ reads exactly half of A₁, because the current splits into equal parts at a junction.

items.q: In the circuit shown, ammeter A₁ reads 3.0 A. What is the reading on ammeter A₂?
items.why:
Adding is the first combination rule learned and the simplest; students also feel that 'more resistors means more resistance' without considering that a second branch is an extra path for the current. A second parallel branch adds a path for the current, so the total current rises and the combined resistance falls. Use the reciprocal rule and check that R_p is less than every branch resistance.

Working: 1/R_p = 1/3.0 + 1/6.0, so R_p = 2.0 Ω. The pd across the parallel pair is V = IR_p = 3.0 A × 2.0 Ω = 6.0 V. A₂ is in the 6.0 Ω branch: I = V/R = 6.0/6.0 = 1.0 A. Check: 6.0/3.0 = 2.0 A in the other branch, and 2.0 + 1.0 = 3.0 A.

items.q: The circuit shown is a potential divider made from an NTC thermistor and a fixed resistor R connected across a supply of constant pd. The voltmeter is ideal. The temperature of the thermistor rises. What happens to the voltmeter reading?
items.correct: It increases, because the resistance of the thermistor falls, so that R takes a larger share of the supply pd.
items.misconception: It decreases, because the resistance of the thermistor rises when it is heated, just as a metal's does.
items.why: Students learn that metals' resistance increases with temperature (the filament lamp) and generalize it to all components. A thermistor is a semiconductor, not a metal. Heating increases the number of mobile charge carriers far more than it increases collisions, so its resistance falls.
items.specStatementText: that resistors can have variable resistance.
items.random_wrong: It stays equal to the supply pd, because the full supply pd appears across each component.

items.q: The graph shows the I–V characteristics of two components, P and Q. Which statement is correct?
items.correct: P obeys Ohm's law, and the resistance of Q increases as the pd across it increases.
items.misconception: The resistance of Q decreases as the pd increases, because the gradient of its graph decreases.
items.why: Both I–V and V–I graphs are used in textbooks, and students remember only 'resistance comes from the gradient', without checking the axes or the units. Check units: a gradient ΔI/ΔV is in A V⁻¹ = Ω⁻¹. Resistance is in V A⁻¹ = Ω. Use R = V/I at the point for any component.
items.specStatementText: the ohmic and non-ohmic behaviour of electrical conductors, including the heating effect of resistors
items.random_wrong: Both P and Q obey Ohm's law, because V = IR can be applied at every point on each graph.

items.q: The graph shows how the terminal pd V of a cell varies with the current I that it delivers. What is the internal resistance of the cell?
items.why:
Both Ir and IR are products of the same current and a resistance, and the phrase 'the pd of the cell' is ambiguous. The terminal pd is the pd across the external circuit, IR. The pd Ir is dissipated inside the cell and never reaches the external circuit.

Working: V = ε − Ir, so the graph of V against I is a straight line with intercept ε and gradient −r. Intercept: ε = 1.5 V. At I = 2.5 A, V = 1.0 V, so r = (ε − V)/I = (1.5 − 1.0)/2.5 = 0.20 Ω.
items.specStatementText: that electric cells are characterized by their emf ε and internal resistance r as given by ε = I(R + r)
items.working: V = ε − Ir, so the graph of V against I is a straight line with intercept ε and gradient −r. Intercept: ε = 1.5 V. At I = 2.5 A, V = 1.0 V, so r = (ε − V)/I = (1.5 − 1.0)/2.5 = 0.20 Ω.

items.q: In the circuit shown, the cell has emf 9.0 V and negligible internal resistance, and the voltmeter is ideal. What does the voltmeter read?
items.why:
In parallel circuits the smaller resistance gets the larger share of the current, and students transfer this inverse rule to pds in series. For series resistances, V₁/V₂ = R₁/R₂ because V = IR with the same I. The inverse rule applies to currents in parallel branches, not to pds in series.

Working: Series: total R = 1.0 + 2.0 + 3.0 = 6.0 Ω, I = 9.0/6.0 = 1.5 A. The voltmeter spans the 1.0 Ω and 2.0 Ω resistors: V = I(R₁ + R₂) = 1.5 × 3.0 = 4.5 V. Equivalently, 9.0 V × 3.0/6.0 = 4.5 V.

items.q: The circuit shows two lamps connected in parallel to a cell of negligible internal resistance. Lamp L₁ has resistance R and lamp L₂ has resistance 2R. Which lamp is brighter, and why?
items.correct: L₁, because the pd across each lamp is the same and P = V²/R is larger for the smaller resistance.
items.misconception: L₁, because the current reaches it first, and only what is then left over passes along to L₂.
items.why: Students follow the arrows on a circuit diagram as if tracing a journey, and water-flow analogies suggest that the water 'gets to' one place before another. The current in a series loop is set by the emf and the total resistance of the whole loop, and it is the same everywhere in it. Position in the loop does not matter: interchanging series components changes nothing.

items.q: The graph shows how the resistance R of a length L of uniform wire varies with L. The cross-sectional area of the wire is 0.50 mm². What is the resistivity of the material of the wire?
items.why:
Students learn the length conversion 1 mm = 10⁻³ m and apply it to areas without squaring the factor. Convert the radius to metres first and then square it; this avoids having to convert an area at all.

Working: R = ρL/A, so the gradient of R against L is ρ/A. Gradient = 0.80 Ω / 2.0 m = 0.40 Ω m⁻¹. A = 0.50 mm² = 0.50 × 10⁻⁶ m². ρ = gradient × A = 0.40 × 5.0 × 10⁻⁷ = 2.0 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m.

items.q: In the potential divider shown, the supply has emf 8.0 V and negligible internal resistance, and the voltmeter is ideal. At the light level in the room the resistance of the LDR is 400 Ω. What does the voltmeter read?
items.why:
In parallel circuits the smaller resistance gets the larger share of the current, and students transfer this inverse rule to pds in series. For series resistances, V₁/V₂ = R₁/R₂ because V = IR with the same I. The inverse rule applies to currents in parallel branches, not to pds in series.

Working: Series: total R = 400 + 1200 = 1600 Ω, I = 8.0/1600 = 5.0 × 10⁻³ A. The voltmeter is across the 1200 Ω resistor: V = IR = 5.0 × 10⁻³ × 1200 = 6.0 V, i.e. 8.0 V × 1200/1600.

items.q: The graph shows how the current I in a wire varies with time t. How much charge passes a point in the wire during the 1.6 s shown?
items.why:
Δq = IΔt is practised only with steady currents, and the largest value on a graph is taken to be 'the current'; the link between the area under an I–t graph and charge is not made. For any current–time graph, charge = area under the graph, just as displacement is the area under a velocity–time graph. For a straight line from the origin, area = ½ × base × height.

Working: I = Δq/Δt, so the charge is the area under the I–t graph. The graph is a straight line from the origin to (1.6 s, 4.0 A): area = ½ × 1.6 s × 4.0 A = 3.2 C.

items.q: Is emf a force?
items.correct: No. Emf is energy transferred per unit charge, measured in volts (J C⁻¹), not a force measured in newtons.
items.misconception: Electromotive force is a force that pushes charges round the circuit, so a 1.5 V cell exerts 1.5 N on each coulomb.
items.why: The historical name 'electromotive force' contains the word 'force', and teachers often describe a cell as 'pushing' charge. Emf is defined as the work done per unit charge by the source, ε = W/q, with unit J C⁻¹ = V. The name is historical. A 1.5 V cell transfers 1.5 J to each coulomb passing through it.
items.specStatementText: that cells provide a source of emf

items.q: Does a solar cell work by using the heat of the Sun?
items.correct: No. A (photovoltaic) solar cell transfers the energy of light directly into electrical energy. Heating the cell does not produce its output; in fact, a hotter cell is slightly less efficient.
items.misconception: A solar cell turns the Sun's heat into electrical energy, in the same way as a solar water-heating panel.
items.why: 'Solar panel' is used in everyday speech for both photovoltaic panels and solar water heaters, and sunlight is experienced mainly as warmth. Photovoltaic cells respond to light: the energy of the incident electromagnetic radiation frees charge carriers in the semiconductor, producing an emf. Solar thermal panels, which heat water, are a different device.
items.specStatementText: chemical cells and solar cells as the energy source in circuits

items.q: Does a renewable source such as a solar cell give a steady output at all times?
items.correct: No. 'Renewable' means the source is not used up; it does not mean it is always available. A solar cell's output varies with light intensity and is zero at night.
items.misconception: Because the Sun never runs out, a solar cell gives a constant output whenever it is needed.
items.why: Energy lessons classify sources as renewable or non-renewable, and students merge 'will not run out' with 'is always available'. Renewability is about whether the resource is replenished, not about reliability. Solar output changes with time of day, weather and season, so solar-powered systems need storage (or another source) to supply energy continuously.

items.q: Can you predict what happens at one point in a circuit by looking only at that point?
items.correct: No. The current in any part of a circuit depends on the whole circuit (the emf and all the resistances in the loop), not only on the components at that point.
items.misconception: Local reasoning: a feature at one place (such as a zero-resistance path across a lamp, or a junction) determines the current there, whatever the rest of the circuit contains.
items.why: Students analyse circuits one component or one junction at a time, and the idea that a 'short circuit' always means a huge current is repeated without its condition (a low total resistance in the loop). Always consider the complete loop. A zero-resistance path gives a large current only if the rest of the loop also has low resistance; if a very high resistance (such as an ideal voltmeter) is in series, the current is negligible however the rest is connected.
items.specStatementText: that circuit diagrams represent the arrangement of components in a circuit

items.q: Does rearranging I = Δq/Δt give Δq = I/Δt?
items.correct: No. Multiplying both sides by Δt gives Δq = IΔt: the charge is the current multiplied by the time.
items.misconception: The charge that flows can be found by dividing the current by the time, Δq = I/Δt (procedural rearrangement error).
items.why: Students rearrange by pattern rather than by operating on both sides, and a quotient in the original equation suggests a quotient in the answer. Rearrange by doing the same operation to both sides: I = Δq/Δt, so IΔt = Δq. Check the units: A × s = (C s⁻¹) × s = C, whereas A/s is not a unit of charge.

items.q: Is conventional current in a metal wire a flow of positive charges?
items.correct: No. In a metal the only mobile carriers are free electrons, which drift from the negative towards the positive terminal. Conventional current is defined as the direction positive charge would flow; the protons in the metal's nuclei do not move along the wire.
items.misconception: Conventional current in a wire is a flow of positive charges (protons) from the positive to the negative terminal.
items.why: Conventional current was defined before the electron was discovered, and diagrams show current arrows from + to − without saying what actually moves. Conventional current is a direction convention. In metals it is carried by electrons moving the opposite way; positive ions are fixed in the lattice. In electrolytes, positive and negative ions both move.

items.q: Is resistance caused by electrons colliding with one another?
items.correct: No. In the IB model, resistance arises from collisions of the free electrons with the lattice ions, which are vibrating about fixed positions; these collisions transfer energy to the lattice.
items.misconception: Resistance comes from the electrons bumping into each other as they crowd through the wire, so more current means more collisions and more resistance.
items.why: Crowd and traffic-jam analogies are used at GCSE for current and resistance, and they suggest that the moving particles obstruct one another. Energy is transferred to the metal (it heats up) because electrons collide with the massive lattice ions. The rate of these collisions increases with temperature, because the ions vibrate with larger amplitude, not because more electrons are moving.

items.q: Does the resistivity of a wire change if it is made longer or thicker?
items.correct: No. Resistivity is a property of the material (at a given temperature). Changing the dimensions changes the resistance, R = ρL/A, but not ρ.
items.misconception: Resistivity is just another name for resistance, so it changes with the length and thickness of the wire in the same way.
items.why: The words 'resistance' and 'resistivity' look alike, and ρ = RA/L contains R, L and A, so students think ρ must change when they do. ρ = RA/L is constant for a given material: if L doubles, R doubles, so RA/L is unchanged. Resistance describes a particular sample; resistivity describes the material.
items.specStatementText: resistivity as given by ρ = RA/L
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does a thicker wire have more resistance than a thinner wire of the same material and length?
items.correct: No. A thicker wire has a larger cross-sectional area, so more charge carriers can flow side by side; its resistance is smaller, R = ρL/A.
items.misconception: A thicker wire has more resistance because there is more material for the current to get through.
items.why: Students picture resistance as an obstacle made of material, so more material means more obstruction; this feels consistent with longer wires having more resistance. Length and area act in opposite ways. A longer path adds more collisions in series (R ∝ L), but a larger area provides more parallel paths for the carriers (R ∝ 1/A). Doubling the diameter quadruples the area and quarters the resistance.
items.specStatementText: resistivity as given by ρ = RA/L
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is power the same as energy?
items.correct: No. Power is the rate of energy transfer (J s⁻¹ = W). The energy transferred in a time t is E = Pt.
items.misconception: Power and energy are the same thing, so the power of a device, in watts, is the energy it transfers, in joules.
items.why: Everyday language uses 'power' and 'energy' interchangeably ('power bills', 'using power'), and electricity bills charge for kilowatt hours, a unit of energy that contains 'watt'. Always ask 'per second?'. A 60 W lamp transfers 60 J every second; in one minute it transfers 3600 J.

items.q: Can the current in a circuit be found using only the external resistance when the cell has internal resistance?
items.correct: No. The total resistance of the loop includes the internal resistance: I = ε/(R + r).
items.misconception: The current can be found from I = ε/R, using the external resistance alone, and the internal resistance used only afterwards (procedural error).
items.why: Students treat internal resistance as a correction to the pd rather than as a resistance in series in the loop, so it is left out when finding the current. Draw the cell as ε in series with r: the same current passes through r and R, so ε = I(R + r). Find I first, then V = IR or V = ε − Ir.
items.specStatementText: that electric cells are characterized by their emf ε and internal resistance r as given by ε = I(R + r)
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does an LDR's resistance increase when more light falls on it?
items.correct: No. An LDR's resistance decreases as light intensity increases, because the light releases more charge carriers; it is highest in darkness.
items.misconception: An LDR 'resists light', so the brighter the light, the greater its resistance.
items.why: The name 'light-dependent resistor' says only that resistance depends on light; students attach 'more light, more resisting' to it, and mix it up with circuits that switch lamps on in the dark. Light energy frees charge carriers in the semiconductor, so the brighter the light, the more carriers and the lower the resistance.
items.specStatementText: that resistors can have variable resistance.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does the component carrying the smallest current have the greatest resistance?
items.correct: Not necessarily. Resistance is the ratio R = V/I; a small current may simply mean a small pd across the component. Only the ratio of pd to current identifies the resistance.
items.misconception: Resistance can be judged from the current alone: the component carrying the least current must have the greatest resistance, whatever pd is across it.
items.why: Students treat current as the primary quantity and resistance as 'what reduces the current', forgetting that the pd across a component also sets its current. Research on circuit reasoning describes this current-centred thinking. Always compute R = V/I with the pd across that component and the current in it. Compare components by the ratio, never by the current or the pd on its own.

items.q: Is the internal resistance of a cell given by the emf divided by the current, r = ε/I?
items.correct: No. ε = I(R + r), so ε/I is the total resistance of the circuit, R + r, not the internal resistance alone. The internal resistance is the lost volts divided by the current, r = (ε − V)/I.
items.misconception: Because the emf belongs to the cell, dividing the emf by the current gives the cell's own resistance: r = ε/I.
items.why: R = V/I is applied by pattern: the cell has a 'voltage' (the emf) and a resistance (r), so the two are divided, ignoring that the emf drives the current through the external resistance as well. Write the loop equation ε = IR + Ir. The pd that belongs to r is only the lost volts Ir = ε − V, so r = (ε − V)/I, which on a graph of terminal pd against current is the magnitude of the gradient.

items.q: Is the drop in terminal pd, ε − V, equal to the internal resistance?
items.correct: No. ε − V is a potential difference, in volts: the 'lost volts' Ir. The internal resistance is this pd divided by the current, r = (ε − V)/I, in ohms.
items.misconception: The internal resistance is the amount by which the terminal pd has fallen below the emf, ε − V (a volt–ohm confusion).
items.why: The lost volts and the internal resistance are introduced together and both describe 'what the cell loses', so the number for one is quoted for the other; on a graph of V against I the fall in V is read off directly as r without dividing by the current. Check units: ε − V is in volts, r in ohms. Divide the lost volts by the current, or take the magnitude of the gradient of the V–I graph, ΔV/ΔI.

items.q: Can an area given in mm² be substituted directly into ρ = RA/L?
items.correct: No. The resistivity comes out in Ω m only if A is in m² and L in m. 1 mm² = 10⁻⁶ m², so an area of 0.50 mm² is 5.0 × 10⁻⁷ m².
items.misconception: A cross-sectional area quoted in mm² can be substituted directly into ρ = RA/L, as if the equation took care of the units (procedural error).
items.why: Wire areas are almost always quoted in mm², and students substitute the number they are given; the mismatch of units is not noticed because the answer is not checked for a sensible order of magnitude. Convert every quantity to base SI units before substituting: 0.50 mm² = 0.50 × 10⁻⁶ m². Metals have resistivities of order 10⁻⁸ to 10⁻⁶ Ω m; a value near 1 Ω m signals a units error.

items.q: A graph of resistance against length for a uniform wire is a straight line through the origin. How is the resistivity found from it?
items.correct: ρ = RA/L, so the gradient of the R–L graph is ρ/A: multiply the gradient by the cross-sectional area (in m²) to obtain ρ, in Ω m.
items.misconception: Resistivity is the resistance per unit length of a wire, ρ = R/L, so it can be read directly as the gradient of a graph of R against L without using the cross-sectional area.
items.why: R ∝ L is the part of R = ρL/A students meet first, so the constant of proportionality on an R–L graph is taken to be the material constant; the units Ω m⁻¹ (gradient) and Ω m (resistivity) look alike and are not checked. The gradient of R against L is ρ/A, not ρ. Resistivity has units Ω m; a resistance per metre has units Ω m⁻¹. Multiply the gradient by A in m².
